title: grid bottlenecks push businesses toward larger onsite power systems capstone 2026 08 24
text:
Aug 24 (Reuters) - Rising demand for onsite power among businesses struggling to secure capacity from strained American utilities is propelling ​orders for larger generation blocks at Capstone Energy+ (CEPL.O)
, opens new tab
, CEO Vince ‌Canino said in an interview with Reuters.
As grid constraints grow, businesses are increasingly viewing onsite generation as a way to secure power for expansion rather ​than simply a means of reducing energy costs.
Capstone, which ​provides microturbine and behind-the-meter power systems for commercial and ⁠industrial customers, is seeing demand from sectors including healthcare and ​is pursuing data-center projects.
"Today's discussions are truly about energy certainty," Canino ​said.
Capstone is now seeing customers buy larger blocks of power, including 3, 4 and 6-megawatt systems, compared with smaller projects that were more typical in ​the past, Canino said.
A 1-megawatt power system can typically supply ​electricity to roughly 750-1,000 homes at a given time, depending on average household ‌demand ⁠and location.
Customers are also moving faster to secure onsite power as they face delays in obtaining utility capacity.
"I think today a lot of those cycles are shrinking because it's no longer about, ​well, is this ​a really good ⁠investment and what's the return? It's more about I need power and I've got to make ​sure I have it on demand," Canino said.
Capstone ​recently ⁠installed a 2 MW combined heat and power system at Scripps Mercy Hospital in San Diego, providing electricity and backup power during ⁠outages.
The company ​has deployed its technology at small ​enterprise data centers but has yet to deploy it at a large-scale data center, ​Canino said.
